rationale: The entry's core identification—that the four winds are the four spirits of heaven, God's executing agents—is carried directly by the printed proof text: Zechariah 6:5 explicitly says 'These are the four spirits of the heavens, which go forth from standing before the Lord of all the earth,' where 'spirits' translates ruach, the same word rendered 'wind.' The directional-merism counter cannot explain why the angel identifies chariots and horses (personal, dispatched agents) as the four ruach, why they 'go forth from standing before the Lord' and return to report (Zech 1:11), or why in Revelation 7:1 the winds can be 'held' by angels and can 'hurt' the earth—compass directions cannot be restrained, commissioned, or do harm. The book's reading incorporates the directional insight (four marks the reach across the quarters) rather than denying it, so it explains everything the merism explains plus the agent-language the merism leaves unexplained. The secondary link to the four horsemen is well supported: Zechariah's four spirit-chariots are drawn by colored horses (red, black, white, pale/grisled) and 'go forth,' and Revelation 6's four colored horses likewise 'go forth' one by one on throne-commissioned errands dealing Ezekiel's four sore judgments—an established intertextual parallel. The Eden-river assertion is a modest pattern claim, and the printed texts literally exhibit it: one river goes out from Eden (the place of God's presence) and parts into four heads (Gen 2:10), matching the fourfold going-out from before the Lord, with Rev 22:1 showing the river proceeding from the throne. Every material assertion actually printed in the entry is supported by the printed references.
book_core_identification: The four winds are the four spirits of heaven (Zech 6:5): commissioned spirit-agents dispatched from God's throne to execute His will across the whole earth—agents sent across the four quarters, not the quarters themselves and not mere weather.
book_secondary_elaborations: The four spirits are shown in the New Testament as the four horsemen of Revelation 6:1-8, commissioned as the Lamb opens the seals.

The same fourfold outgoing pattern (one source at God's presence parting four ways to reach the earth) appears in the river that went out of Eden and parted into four heads (Gen 2:10), with the throne-river of Rev 22:1 as the corresponding image.
chapter_only_objections: The claim that the seals 'commission but do not release' the riders, with the winds still held at the sixth seal (harmonizing Rev 6 and Rev 7:1-3), is a chapter-level chronological argument not asserted in the entry and is contestable.
The chapter's typological chain linking garment corners, Numbers 15:39, and the remnant of Rev 12:17 ('the winds gather from the hem those who kept the hem') is speculative and not part of the entry.

The chapter's handling of texts like Dan 8:8/11:4 ('toward the four winds' as plain directional idiom) is thin; the agent reading is strained in those distributive-direction texts, though the chapter's concession that 'four' marks the quarters absorbs most of the difficulty.
The east-wind 'compass habit' section and the Pentecost/Ezekiel 37 fulfillment claim are chapter applications beyond the entry's scope.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The mainstream reading: 'the four winds' is a stock ancient Near Eastern merism for the four cardinal directions, meaning 'everywhere / the whole earth.' Phrases like 'from/toward the four winds' simply denote universal scope of scattering or gathering; where winds act (Jer 49:36; Dan 7:2; Rev 7:1), they are contextually colored as destructive forces under God's control, but the base referent is directional, not a class of spirit-beings.
counter_core_identification: The four winds are an idiom for the four compass points—universal geographic extent—not identifiable agents; any agency in context belongs to God acting everywhere, not to four commissioned spirits.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that 'the four winds' refers to beings at all: directions and dispatched spirit-agents cannot both be the core referent of the same expression. If the winds are merely compass points, the entry's identification of them as God's executing agents shown as the four horsemen is false.
counter_case: 'Toward the four winds of heaven' in Dan 8:8 and 11:4 reads naturally as pure directional idiom (a kingdom divided in all directions), which is awkward for an agent reading.
Matt 24:31/Mark 13:27 pair 'from the four winds' with 'from one end of heaven to the other,' an explicitly spatial gloss.
Akkadian and broader ANE usage attests 'four winds' as a conventional directional merism.
In Rev 7:1 the winds are distinguished from the four angels who hold them, suggesting the winds are forces controlled by agents rather than agents themselves.
book_explanatory_advantages: Zech 6:5 explicitly identifies the four ruach as things that 'go forth from standing before the Lord'—personal commission language impossible for compass directions.

The Zech 6 chariots drawn by colored horses map tightly onto the four colored horsemen of Rev 6, both going forth on throne-issued errands; the directional reading has no account of this cross-text parallel.
Rev 7:1's winds that must be 'held' lest they 'hurt' the earth, sea, and trees are agents/forces with destructive capacity, not directions.
The horsemen's portfolio (sword, famine, death, beasts, Rev 6:8) matches Ezekiel's four sore judgments, giving the fourfold agents a defined executive office.
The book's core subsumes the counter's strength: 'four' marks coverage of the quarters, so directional texts remain explicable while agent texts also are.
The Eden river (Gen 2:10) and throne river (Rev 22:1) supply an independent witness to the fourfold going-out-from-the-presence pattern the entry asserts.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Cleanest reading of the distributive-direction texts (Dan 8:8; 11:4; Zech 2:6) where winds are destinations, not actors.
Matches attested ANE idiom and the explicit spatial gloss in Matt 24:31.
In Rev 7:1 it avoids identifying the winds as agents when separate angels do the holding.
decisive_sources: Zechariah 6:5 (chariots explicitly named 'the four spirits of the heavens, which go forth from standing before the Lord')
Revelation 6:1-8 (four colored horses going forth on commissioned errands, paralleling Zechariah's colored horse-chariots)
Genesis 2:10 with Revelation 22:1 (one source at the presence parted four ways—the fourfold outgoing pattern the entry asserts)
Psalm 104:4 as cited in the chapter ('who maketh his angels spirits'—ruach as commissioned ministers)
unresolved_objections: The agent reading remains strained in purely distributive texts such as Dan 8:8 and 11:4, though the entry's texts do not include them and the book's concession that 'four' marks the quarters mitigates the tension.

Rev 7:1 distinguishes the holding angels from the held winds, which slightly complicates a simple winds-equal-angels equation, though it still requires the winds to be harmful active forces rather than directions.
